fix.summary: Give this statement more sort memory (64MB instead of 4MB, if the application's role doesn't already set more), for the role the application connects as or only around this statement, rather than server-wide; or add an index that returns rows already in the order the sort needs, or sort fewer rows. findings.summary: A sort or hash in this statement needs more memory than work_mem (4MB in Culprit's session; a setting on the application's role or database can differ) and writes the overflow to temporary files: 4.2 GB over 214 runs. pg_stat_statements counts the total, so whether every run spills or only some is unknown. Writing temp files and reading them back is many times slower than sorting in memory. Each run also sends 247K rows (≈ 17.4 MB) to the application, and few screens or jobs need that many at once: returning fewer can keep the sort in memory too.

caveats: The update behind most of these ran once in the 5 hours since statistics were reset: a backfill or a migration looks like this, and its share stays in the counts long after. It needs work only if updates like it keep coming.

How long these counts have run isn't known (PostgreSQL 15+ records no start until its statistics are first reset, and the counts outlive restarts): one large update or backfill long ago would keep the share low. fix.summary: Leave room on each page so updated rows fit next to the old version: a fillfactor of 85–90 is typical for tables updated often. It applies to pages written from now on; existing pages get the room as rows move (pg_repack rewrites the table online if you want it at once). If an index covers a column that changes on every update (updated_at, status, counters), dropping it makes those updates HOT too.

findings.summary: An update that changes no indexed column and finds room on the same page is HOT: it writes no index entries and its old version is cleaned up without VACUUM. None of wide's 21K updates were, so each wrote a new entry in both of its indexes. 100% of them moved to another page because their own was full (fillfactor 100). An update of wide changed 21K of these rows and wrote 174 MB of WAL for them, about 8.3 KB a row: an update that isn't HOT logs the new row version and an entry in every index, and the first change to each page after a checkpoint logs the whole page.
